analysis.one_liner: Bans nearly all manufacture, sale, and private possession of handguns, with narrow exceptions.
analysis.headline: The handgun ban bill drew zero cosponsors and died in a House Judiciary subcommittee without ever reaching a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it a federal crime to make, sell, buy, own, possess, transport, or use a handgun or handgun ammunition. Military, police, registered security guard services, and licensed target-shooting clubs would be exempt. People who turned in their handguns within 180 days would get at least $25 or the gun's fair market value; after that, handing a gun over would avoid prosecution but carry a civil fine of up to $500.
analysis.who_benefits: Under the bill's own findings, residents of communities affected by handgun violence: the bill cites handgun homicides setting annual records since 1987 and $20.4 billion in annual medical and productivity costs from handgun violence. Police, the military, registered security firms, and licensed target clubs would keep their handguns by exemption.

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares that handgun homicides set new records every year after 1987 and that handgun violence costs the economy about $20.4 billion a year in medical spending and lost productivity [S3].

It would outlaw the full chain of handgun commerce — manufacture, import, sale, purchase, transfer, and possession — except for the armed forces, law enforcement, registered security guard services, and licensed handgun clubs and their members [S2][S3].
Owners could voluntarily turn in handguns to any designated law enforcement agency and receive the greater of $25 or fair market value if they did so within 180 days [S2][S3].

The bill states that guns kept at home are more likely to endanger the people living there than to protect them, and that handguns in schools force districts to divert money to security equipment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Current handgun owners, who would have to surrender or lose their guns — the bill estimated more than 75 million privately held handguns at the time. Gun and ammunition makers, importers, and dealers would lose nearly their entire handgun business, and target shooters outside licensed clubs could no longer keep handguns at home.
analysis.who_pays_short: Handgun owners and the gun industry

drawbacks.text: The ban would reach tens of millions of law-abiding owners: the bill itself counts privately held handguns at more than 75 million, rising by 2.5 million a year, and offers owners only $25 or fair market value to turn them in [S3].

The exceptions are narrow. A person could only keep a handgun as a member of a licensed target club, and even then the club must store it at the club or with police when not in use — so home possession for self-defense would end for everyone outside the exempted groups [S3].

Possessing a handgun after the 180-day grace period would carry up to five years in prison, and the bill relies on federal recordkeeping, licensing, and forfeiture machinery that would take substantial enforcement resources to run [S2][S3].

Many Americans regard handgun ownership as a constitutional right, and a near-total ban faced certain legal and political challenge (general knowledge about the Second Amendment debate, not from the provided sources).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If the bill's findings are right — record handgun homicides and $20.4 billion in annual costs — the public-health payoff would be large and the cost to the country small relative to it. But the burden falls heavily and immediately on tens of millions of current owners, the compensation offered is modest, and the design (a near-total ban with club-based storage) was the most aggressive version of handgun regulation available, which helps explain why it attracted no support even in a Congress still open to some gun legislation.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, sent to its Crime Subcommittee in March 1995, and never moved again before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Major Owens introduced the bill on February 13, 1995, with no cosponsors [S1][S4][S5].
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day [S5].
On March 15, 1995, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, where the record ends [S5].
No markup, floor action, or vote ever occurred, and the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Handgun makers, dealers, and existing owners — the status quo they preferred continued unchanged.

for.name: Rep. Major Owens
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; it was his sole sponsorship, with no cosponsors

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on February 13, 1995 and never reported it out or scheduled action on it

against.name: Subcommittee on Crime
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 15, 1995 and took no further action on the bill

against.name: National Rifle Association and allied gun-rights groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed proposals to ban or severely restrict handguns during this period, making a near-total handgun ban politically untouchable

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no one else sponsored the bill, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor in a Republican-controlled House and no measurable support from either party.

industries.note: The bill would criminalize the manufacture, import, and sale of handguns and handgun ammunition except to supply exempted police, military, security, and club customers — ending the civilian handgun market that the bill says was adding 2.5 million guns a year. The industry's interest in the bill's defeat ran directly against the public-safety goal the bill pursued [S2][S3].
Dealers and importers could operate only as narrow conduits for exempt buyers under Treasury-approved transactions, eliminating retail handgun sales to the general public [S2][S3].

Security firms are carved out of the ban entirely and become one of the few private channels allowed to possess handguns, in exchange for a $50 annual registration fee, storage rules, and recordkeeping. The bill locks in their privileged access while everyone outside the exempted groups loses it [S3].

Clubs that meet storage, supervision, and licensing rules become the only private place a civilian handgun can exist, with a $25 annual fee — the bill entrenches them as the sole legal home for sport shooting while banning individual ownership [S3].
